title: Hidden Among Supernovae
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 1058, imaged by the Gemini North telescope
credit: International Gemini Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA · Image processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), J. Miller (Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab), M. Rodriguez (Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab) & M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A luminous centre and arms streaked with blues and pinks mark NGC 1058, a quiet-looking spiral galaxy imaged by the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph (GMOS) on Gemini North. The colours along its arms indicate active regions of star formation. In the night sky, the galaxy appears roughly as bright as Proxima Centauri.

Its calm appearance hides a record of starbursts and supernovae. NGC 1058 is a Seyfert Type 2 galaxy, a type with an active, bright centre, and it belongs to the NGC 1023 Group in the constellation Perseus. Astronomers have observed three supernovae there, SN 1961V, SN 1969L and SN 2007gr.

The first of these, SN 1961V, remains a mystery. A faint expanding shell of gas can just be made out, but some astronomers doubt it was a true supernova, because a bright star still shines near the spot. As the supposed explosion slowly fades, that suspect star keeps shining, dimming unusually slowly.
scale: NGC 1058 lies about 30 million light-years away, according to NOIRLab.

understand.summary: Taken in visible and near-infrared light with GMOS on Gemini North through g, r, i, z and hydrogen-alpha filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The long exposure gathers far more light than the eye, bringing out the faint arms and their star-forming regions.
